title: US Private Sector Adds Just 38,000 Jobs in August, Missing Forecasts
excerpt: ADP report shows the slowest pace of private-sector hiring since January, with manufacturing and professional services shedding jobs even as education and health care expanded.
body:
• U.S. private employers added just 38,000 jobs in August, falling short of the 47,000-48,000 economists had expected and marking the slowest pace of hiring since January
  • Education and health services was a bright spot at 45,000 new positions, while manufacturing shed 17,000 jobs and professional services lost 16,000
  • Large companies with 500 or more employees drove most of the gains, adding 34,000 jobs, while mid-sized firms were flat and small businesses added only 3,000
  • The report sets the stage for Friday's Bureau of Labor Statistics employment report, where economists expect 53,000 to 56,000 total nonfarm payroll additions

Hiring Momentum Slows Across Key Sectors

U.S. private-sector hiring decelerated sharply in August, with employers adding just 38,000 jobs — below forecasts and the weakest monthly gain since January — according to the ADP National Employment Report released Wednesday.

Economists surveyed by Reuters had forecast 48,000 new jobs, while The Wall Street Journal's panel expected 47,000. July's figure was revised upward to 46,000 from an initially reported 44,000, but the downward trajectory raised fresh concerns about labor market softening.

The report, produced by ADP Research in collaboration with the Stanford Digital Economy Lab, highlighted a widening divergence between service-sector strength and goods-producing weakness.

Winners and Losers by Industry

Service-providing industries added 48,000 positions overall, led by education and health services at 45,000 — a figure that single-handedly exceeded the total net job gain. Leisure and hospitality contributed 16,000, while financial activities added 6,000.

Goods-producing sectors shed a net 10,000 jobs. Manufacturing was the biggest drag, losing 17,000 positions. Natural resources and mining lost 5,000, while construction was a lone bright spot among goods producers, adding 12,000 jobs.

Professional and business services — a bellwether for white-collar employment — lost 16,000 positions, while trade, transportation and utilities and the information sector also contracted.

"Pay can tell us a lot about today's choppy hiring. To understand hiring patterns, you have to look deeply into where pay growth is accelerating, where it's slowing, and for whom."

— Dr. Nela Richardson, Chief Economist, ADP

Big Companies Drive the Gains

The size breakdown underscored a top-heavy labor market. Large businesses with 500 or more employees added 34,000 jobs, accounting for the vast majority of August's net gains. Mid-sized companies with 50 to 499 employees recorded zero net hiring. Small businesses with fewer than 50 workers added just 3,000 positions.

Pay growth for workers who stayed in their jobs held steady at 3% year over year, while compensation growth for job-changers edged lower. Annual pay was up 4.7% overall, ADP reported.

Labor Market in 'Slow-Hire, Slow-Fire' Mode

Economists continued to characterize the labor market as being in a "slow-hire, slow-fire" state, with momentum fading from a spring rebound. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday that there were 1.05 open jobs for every unemployed person in July, essentially unchanged from June.

Several headwinds are weighing on job creation. The six-month U.S.-Israeli war with Iran is straining supply chains and keeping input prices elevated. Immigration policy changes, including deportations and cancelled work authorizations, may also be limiting payroll growth. The recent end of Temporary Protected Status for hundreds of thousands of Haitians has created additional downside risks.

"Immigration policy changes likely held back payrolls growth in August. AI is having less of an effect on hiring than other factors like reduced immigration or tariff whiplash."

— Bill Adams, Chief Economist, Fifth Third Commercial Bank

Eyes Turn to Friday's Government Report

The ADP data is a prelude to Friday's more comprehensive BLS employment report. Economists expect nonfarm payrolls to have rebounded by 53,000 to 56,000 jobs after a surprise 23,000-job decline in July, partly reflecting a recovery in local government education hiring. The unemployment rate is forecast to hold at 4.1%.

ADP's track record as a predictor of the BLS figure is mixed, and markets typically treat it as a sentiment indicator rather than a precise forecast. Factory orders, also released Wednesday, rebounded 0.9% in July after a 0.2% decline in June, driven by a 12.7% surge in civilian aircraft orders.
